The invisibility cloak conceals a macroscopic object up to 2 mm tall, over 3500 wavelengths at visible light.
The cloak is made from two pieces of natural calcite crystals cemented back-to-back.
Calcite's birefringence provides two principal refractive indices: approximately 1.48 and 1.66 for green light at 561 nm.
The cloak operates in a transparent liquid environment with refractive index about 1.57.
The design uses transformation optics to guide light around the object, restoring both reflection angle and position.
The cloak works for light polarized with magnetic field parallel to the horizontal plane.
The cloak's geometry is trapezoidal with a small triangular indentation underneath to hide the object.
Experimental validation used laser diodes at wavelengths 488 nm (blue), 561 nm (green), and 650 nm (red).
Color aberrations cause small lateral shifts (~4-5% of object height) at blue and red wavelengths.
The cloak was tested at incident angles of 0°, 18°, and 40°, with best performance at lower angles.
The cloak eliminates energy loss issues associated with metal-based metamaterials.
The cloak was fabricated using conventional optical lens fabrication techniques and low-cost materials.
The bottom surface of the cloak was polished and coated with silver to serve as a reflective ground plane.
The cloak can hide any object smaller than the steel wedge placed under it.
The cloak currently works only in 2D geometry and for a single polarization.
The cloak's anisotropic refractive indices are designed by diagonalizing the permittivity tensor derived from the coordinate transformation.
The cloak's crystal axis orientation is approximately 37.5° relative to the vertical plane for green light.
The front, back, and top surfaces of the cloak were painted black to absorb scattered light.
The cloak design avoids the lateral shift problem found in quasiconformal carpet cloaks.
The cloak was experimentally shown to transform a deformed mirror surface into a flat one from the observer's perspective.
